title: OA 3 — Core Practice (Medium)
description: Medium mock data-science internship assessment: CS/AI/ML/statistics/testing MCQs, aptitude, chart-based data analysis, SQL, pandas and DSA.
disclaimer: Independent practice material informed by publicly reported role requirements and general internship-assessment patterns. Not official Nasdaq questions.

revealPolicy.rule: Never send private fields to the candidate before the whole attempt has finished.

sections.title: Section 1: CS Fundamentals, AI, ML, Statistics and Testing

questions.statement: For a k-nearest-neighbours classifier the team recorded: k=1 → train error 0%, 5-fold CV error 22%; k=15 → train 12%, CV 14%; k=200 → train 25%, CV 26%. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: k=1 is best because its training error is lowest
k=200 is best because its training and CV errors are nearly equal
All three are equivalent because CV error is always higher than training error
k=1 overfits (high variance); k=200 underfits (high bias); k=15 gives the best bias-variance trade-off of the three

solution.explanation: Choose by validation/CV error, not training error. k=1 memorises noise (0% train, 22% CV). k=200 is too smooth so even training error is high (high bias). Similar train and CV error alone does not mean the model is good if both are high.

hints: Compare training and validation error; choose by validation error.

questions.statement: A classifier has ROC AUC = 0.82 on a held-out set. Which statement is correct?

options.text: 82% of all predictions are correct at every threshold
If you pick one random positive and one random negative case, the model scores the positive higher about 82% of the time
The model is guaranteed to be calibrated
The model has a precision of 0.82 at the 0.5 threshold

solution.explanation: AUC is the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative. It is threshold-independent, says nothing about precision at a specific cut-off, and does not imply calibrated probabilities.

hints: AUC = probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative.

questions.statement: Why does a random forest usually generalise better than a single deep decision tree trained on the same data?

options.text: Random forests always have lower training error than a single tree
Each tree in the forest is shallower, which removes all bias
Averaging many trees trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets reduces variance without greatly increasing bias
The forest uses the test set to prune trees

solution.explanation: Deep trees have low bias but high variance. Bagging plus feature subsampling decorrelates the trees so their averaged prediction is more stable. The forest does not remove bias, never touches the test set, and its training error is not guaranteed to be lower.

hints: Averaging many decorrelated models reduces variance.

questions.statement: In a random forest each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of n rows (sampling with replacement). For large n, roughly what fraction of rows is left out of a given tree's sample (and available for out-of-bag evaluation)?

options.text: Exactly 0%, since every row is sampled at least once

solution.explanation: P(a given row is never drawn in n draws) = (1 − 1/n)^n → e^−1 ≈ 0.368. About 63.2% of rows are in the bootstrap sample; the rest provide a built-in validation estimate (OOB error).

hints: P(not picked in n draws) = (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → e⁻¹.

questions.statement: How does an Isolation Forest decide that a point is anomalous?

options.text: Anomalies are isolated by random splits in fewer steps, so they have shorter average path lengths in the trees
Anomalies are the points with the longest path length in the trees
Anomalies are the points farthest from the global mean in every feature
Anomalies are points that the forest classifies with the lowest accuracy

solution.explanation: Isolation Forest repeatedly splits randomly on features; rare, different points are separated quickly (short paths), while dense normal points need many splits.

hints: Random splits isolate rare points quickly — do anomalies need more or fewer splits?

questions.statement: You are forecasting next-day volatility from three years of daily data. Which validation scheme is most appropriate for choosing hyper-parameters?

options.text: Train on the most recent year and test on the oldest year
Validate on the training data, since time series are autocorrelated
Walk-forward (expanding or rolling window) validation: always train on the past and validate on a later block
Standard shuffled 5-fold cross-validation, because it uses all data efficiently

solution.explanation: Shuffled folds put future observations in the training set and past ones in validation, leaking information and giving optimistic scores. Walk-forward validation mimics production: only past data can be used to predict the future.

hints: Training data must always come from BEFORE the validation data.

questions.statement: A logistic regression without regularization is fitted to training data in which one feature perfectly separates the two classes. What typically happens?

options.text: The maximum-likelihood coefficient grows without bound (the optimiser does not converge to a finite solution); a regularization penalty keeps it finite
The model automatically drops that feature

solution.explanation: With perfect separation the likelihood keeps improving as the weight grows, so no finite maximiser exists. L2 (or L1) regularization adds a penalty that yields finite coefficients.

hints: If a feature separates the classes perfectly, does the likelihood keep improving as the weight grows?

questions.statement: Daily returns of a stock are modelled as Normal with mean 0.10% and standard deviation 1.50%. Approximately what is the probability that tomorrow's return is below −1.90%?

solution.explanation: z = (−1.90 − 0.10)/1.50 = −1.333, and Φ(−1.333) ≈ 0.091. Forgetting to subtract the mean (z = −1.27) or using the wrong tail gives other options; 18.2% would be a two-sided probability.

hints: z = (x − μ)/σ, then use the normal table: Φ(−1.33) ≈ 0.09.

questions.statement: 10% of news articles are negative-sentiment. 30% of negative articles contain the word 'lawsuit' versus 5% of non-negative articles. If an article contains 'lawsuit', what is the probability it is negative?

solution.explanation: P(neg|lawsuit) = 0.10·0.30 / (0.10·0.30 + 0.90·0.05) = 0.03/0.075 = 0.40. 30% is the likelihood P(lawsuit|neg), not the posterior.

hints: Bayes: P(neg|word) = P(word|neg)P(neg) / P(word); P(word) = 0.1·0.3 + 0.9·0.05.

questions.statement: A sentiment label X takes values −1, 0, +1 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. What is Var(X)?

solution.explanation: E[X] = −0.2 + 0 + 0.3 = 0.1; E[X²] = 0.2 + 0 + 0.3 = 0.5; Var = 0.5 − 0.1² = 0.49. 0.50 forgets to subtract the squared mean.

hints: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².

questions.statement: In a sample of 400 articles, 120 are classified as positive. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the true proportion positive (normal approximation)?

In a 2×2 table of article sentiment (positive/negative) by source type (wire/blog), row totals are 100 (positive) and 300 (negative), column totals are 150 (wire) and 250 (blog), total N = 400. What is the expected count for positive–wire under independence?

solution.explanation: Expected = (row total × column total) / N = 100·150/400 = 37.5. The chi-square statistic sums (O − E)²/E over cells.

hints: Expected count = (row total × column total) / grand total.

questions.statement: To detect a true mean shift of 2 units with a one-sample two-sided z-test (σ = 10, α = 0.05, desired power 80%, z-values 1.96 and 0.84), what sample size is needed?

solution.explanation: n = ((z_{α/2} + z_β)·σ/δ)² = ((1.96 + 0.84)·10/2)² = 14² = 196. 784 would result from using δ = 1; 49 from forgetting to square the (σ/δ) ratio correctly.

hints: n = ((z_α/2 + z_β) σ / δ)².

questions.statement: A loan model approves 60% of applicants from group X and 40% from group Y, but among truly creditworthy applicants both groups are approved at the same rate (equal true positive rate). Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Equal opportunity (equal TPR) holds, but demographic parity (equal approval rates) does not
Both demographic parity and equal opportunity hold
Demographic parity holds because the TPRs match

solution.explanation: Demographic parity compares overall positive-decision rates (60% vs 40% → violated). Equal opportunity compares TPR among truly positive individuals (equal → satisfied). Different fairness criteria can disagree, so the choice must be justified for the use case.

hints: Compare approval rates overall (demographic parity) vs. among truly positive cases (equal opportunity).

questions.statement: A customer disputes why their individual transaction was blocked. Which kind of explanation best serves this request?

options.text: A local, per-prediction explanation (e.g., SHAP values or a counterfactual: "approved if amount were below X")
A global feature-importance bar chart averaged over all customers
The model's overall accuracy on the test set

solution.explanation: The question concerns one decision, so a local explanation that attributes that single prediction (or offers a counterfactual) is appropriate. Global importance describes the model on average and does not justify one decision.

hints: One decision → global or local explanation?

questions.statement: Why do transformer models need positional encodings (or equivalent position information)?

options.text: To reduce the dimensionality of the embeddings
To allow the model to process only short sentences
Self-attention by itself treats the input as an unordered set, so word order information must be injected explicitly
To make attention weights sum to one

solution.explanation: Attention computes pairwise interactions without any inherent order, so 'A beat B' and 'B beat A' would look identical without position information. Softmax already normalises attention weights.

hints: Attention treats its inputs as a set — what information is missing?

questions.statement: A RAG assistant for financial filings sometimes answers with outdated figures even though the correct filing is in the index. Which diagnostic step is most useful first?

options.text: Fine-tune the model on the questions asked so far, without checking retrieval
Increase the generator's temperature to get more varied answers
Measure retrieval quality separately (e.g., recall@k of the right passage); if the right chunk is missing from the top-k, fix chunking/metadata filters/reranking before changing the generator
Delete the index and rely only on the model's parametric memory

solution.explanation: RAG quality depends on both retrieval and generation. If the correct passage is not retrieved, no generator can ground its answer in it; evaluating each stage separately localises the failure. Higher temperature increases randomness, not grounding.

hints: Two stages: retrieval and generation. Which one fails if the right passage is never retrieved?

questions.statement: A summarisation model writes a fluent quote attributed to a CEO that does not appear in the source article. Which mitigation is most appropriate for a production newsroom tool?

options.text: Make the prompt longer and more polite
Set temperature to 0, which guarantees that hallucinations cannot occur
Ground generation in the source, require citations/quote verification against the text, and keep a human review step for high-stakes outputs
Remove all source documents so the model relies on its own knowledge

solution.explanation: Hallucinated content is plausible but unsupported. Lower temperature can reduce variability but offers no guarantee; grounding, automated checks against sources and human oversight address the risk.

hints: Which mitigation ties the output to verifiable sources, with a human check for high stakes?

questions.statement: A composite index exists on Transactions(account_id, txn_time). Which query can use the index efficiently for an index range scan?

solution.explanation: A B-tree composite index is ordered by its leading column first. Seeking on account_id and then ranging on txn_time uses it fully; predicates that skip the leading column or involve other columns cannot use it for a seek (leftmost-prefix rule).

hints: Composite B-tree indexes work from the leftmost column onwards.

questions.statement: A `RiskReport` class needs the ability to format numbers using the existing `Formatter` class. Which design is generally preferable?

options.text: Give RiskReport a Formatter field (composition), because a report is not a kind of formatter
Make all Formatter methods static and extend them in each report
Copy the Formatter code into every report class
Make RiskReport extend Formatter, since this reuses the code

solution.explanation: Inheritance should model an 'is-a' relationship; reuse alone is better achieved by composition ('has-a'), which keeps coupling lower and avoids exposing unrelated inherited methods.

hints: 'Is-a' (inheritance) vs 'has-a' (composition): is a report a formatter?

questions.statement: Scores in descending order are 90, 90, 80. Which window function assigns the ranks 1, 1, 2 respectively?

solution.explanation: DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same rank without gaps (1,1,2). RANK leaves a gap after ties (1,1,3); ROW_NUMBER numbers rows uniquely (1,2,3).

hints: RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not.

questions.statement: An article can mention many entities and an entity can appear in many articles, with a sentiment score per mention. What is the standard relational design?

options.text: Add one entity_id column to Articles
Store a comma-separated list of entity ids in an Articles column
Duplicate the article text for each entity in the Entities table
A junction table (article_id, entity_id, score) with a composite primary key (article_id, entity_id) and foreign keys to both parents

solution.explanation: Many-to-many relationships are modelled with an associative table keyed by both foreign keys; lists in a column violate first normal form and make joins and constraints hard.

hints: Many-to-many relationships need a third (junction) table.

questions.statement: A sentiment model should not change its prediction when a company name in the text is replaced by another company name. Which kind of test checks this?

options.text: A test that predictions are exactly equal to the training labels
A boundary test of the learning rate
An invariance (perturbation) test: apply a label-preserving change and assert the prediction does not change
A load test of the server

solution.explanation: Behavioural ML testing includes invariance tests (label-preserving perturbations), directional-expectation tests and minimum-functionality tests, which reveal brittle or biased behaviour that aggregate accuracy hides.

hints: A label-preserving change should leave the prediction unchanged — what is that test called?

questions.statement: Consider `if (x > 0 && y > 0) { A(); } else { B(); }`. Which pair of tests gives 100% branch (decision) coverage?

options.text: x = 1, y = 1 (takes the true branch) and x = −1, y = 1 (takes the false branch)

solution.explanation: Branch coverage needs the decision to evaluate to both true and false at least once. Two true tests (or two false tests) cover only one branch.

hints: Branch coverage needs the decision to be true at least once AND false at least once.

questions.statement: A mutation-testing tool creates 10 mutants of the code and the test suite fails (kills) 8 of them. What is the mutation score and what does it mean?

options.text: 80%; the suite detects 80% of the injected faults, so 2 mutants survived and reveal weaknesses or equivalent mutants
20%; the suite is bad because 20% of tests failed
100%; every mutant is by definition detected

solution.explanation: Mutation score = killed mutants / total mutants = 8/10. Surviving mutants point to missing assertions or to mutants that do not change behaviour (equivalent mutants).

hints: Mutation score = killed mutants / total mutants.

questions.statement: The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 5:7. If there are 30 boys, how many students are in the class?
hints: Find the value of one ratio part first.

questions.statement: A sum of 8000 earns simple interest of 3840 in 4 years. What is the annual rate?
A bag has 5 red and 5 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after another without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
hints: Without replacement the second draw has one fewer ball of that colour and one fewer ball overall.

questions.statement: The average weight of 8 players is 40 kg. A player weighing 30 kg leaves and another weighing 40 kg joins. What is the new average?

solution.explanation: New total = 320 − 30 + 40 = 330; divide by 8: 41.25 kg.

hints: Replace the individual in the total, not in the average, then divide by the (unchanged) count.

questions.statement: The length of a rectangle is increased by 20% and its breadth is decreased by 20%. What is the percentage change in its area?

solution.explanation: Area multiplier = 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96. Change = -4%.

hints: Area scales by (1 + p/100)(1 − q/100).

questions.statement: A, B and C can complete a task alone in 6, 12 and 4 days respectively. Working together how many days do they need?
hints: Add the three daily rates, then take the reciprocal.

questions.statement: A share price rises by 10% on Monday and then falls by 40% on Tuesday. What is the net percentage change over the two days?
hints: Successive changes multiply: new = old × (1 + p/100) × (1 − q/100). Don't just add the percentages.

questions.statement: Find the next number: 1, 5, 11, 19, 29, ?

solution.explanation: Differences: 4, 6, 8, 10 — they grow by 2 each time, so the next difference is 12 and the answer is 41.

hints: Take first differences; if they are not constant take second differences.

questions.statement: A father is 2 times as old as his son. 5 years from now the sum of their ages will be 43. How old is the son now?

solution.explanation: Let son = s, father = 2s. After 5 years the sum is 3s + 10 = 43, so s = 11.

hints: Let the son's age be s; write the father's age in terms of s and form one equation.

questions.statement: What is the smaller angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at 3:00?

solution.explanation: Angle = |30h − 5.5m| = |90 − 0| = 90°; the smaller angle is 90°.

hints: Angle = |30h − 5.5m| degrees (take 360 minus it if it exceeds 180).

questions.statement: Farid is not taller than Chen; Gita is taller than Asha; Farid is taller than Esha; Esha is taller than Gita. All heights are different. Who is the 2nd tallest?

solution.explanation: Chain the statements: Chen > Farid > Esha > Gita > Asha (tallest to shortest). The 2nd tallest is Farid.

hints: Arrange the people in a chain from the comparisons, then read off the requested position.

questions.statement: A committee of 2 is to be chosen from 9 people. In how many ways can this be done?

solution.explanation: Order does not matter: 9C2 = 36.

hints: Selection without order: nCr = n! / (r!(n − r)!).

questions.statement: A person travels 120 km at 40 km/h and returns along the same route at 60 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole journey?

solution.explanation: Total distance = 240; total time = 120/40 + 120/60 = 5 h; average = 48 km/h. Not the arithmetic mean.

hints: Average speed = total distance / total time. For equal distances use 2ab/(a + b).

questions.statement: The sum of three consecutive integers is 39. What is the product of the smallest and largest?

solution.explanation: The integers are 12, 13, 14; product of the extremes = 168.

hints: Call the middle integer m; the others are m − 1 and m + 1.

questions.statement: A vessel contains 80 litres of pure milk. 20 litres are removed and replaced by water; then 20 litres of the mixture are removed and replaced by water again. How much milk is left?

solution.explanation: Milk left = 80 × (1 − 20/80)² = 45 litres.

hints: After n replacements: remaining = initial × (1 − removed/total)ⁿ.

questions.statement: What is the difference between the API latency in May and in Feb?
hints: Subtract the smaller value from the larger.

questions.statement: By what percentage did API latency rise from Apr to May?
hints: Percentage change = (new − old) / old × 100 — divide by the earlier value.

questions.statement: What is the average API latency over the six months shown?
hints: Average = sum of the six values / 6.

questions.statement: What was the revenue per employee (in $M, to 2 decimals) in Q3?
hints: Combine the charts: revenue ÷ headcount for the same quarter.

questions.statement: By how much (in $M, 2 decimals) did revenue per employee change from Q1 to Q5? (Answer: Q5 value − Q1 value.)
hints: Compute revenue ÷ headcount for both quarters, then subtract.

questions.statement: In which quarter was revenue per employee the highest?

solution.explanation: Revenue per employee: Q1: 1.94, Q2: 2.00, Q3: 2.87, Q4: 3.20, Q5: 3.00. Highest: Q4.

hints: Compute revenue ÷ headcount for each quarter; highest revenue is not necessarily the best productivity.

questions.statement: What percentage of the cloud bill do Licences and Storage account for together?
hints: Shares of the same whole can be added.

questions.statement: How many times as large is the share of Support compared with the share of Compute? (Answer to 2 decimals.)
hints: Divide the larger share by the smaller one.

questions.statement: The total cloud bill is 240 $K. How much is Network?
hints: Amount = share% × total.

charts.title: Cloud spend: Product X vs Product Y

hints: Compute |series 1 − series 2| for each category.

questions.statement: From 2019 to 2024, which series grew by the larger percentage, and by how much (approx.)?

charts.title: Cloud spend: Product X vs Product Y

hints: Percentage growth = (last − first)/first × 100, computed for each series.

questions.statement: In which year were Product X and Product Y closest to each other?

charts.title: Cloud spend: Product X vs Product Y

questions.title: Flag Rate per Model Run
questions.statement:
MLOps wants a monitoring table for every model run, including runs that produced no usable predictions. Use `ModelRuns` and `Predictions`.

For **every** run return:

`run_id, model_name, version, n_predictions, n_flagged, flag_rate, avg_score`

* `n_predictions` – predictions of the run with a **non-NULL** `score`
* `n_flagged` – those with `score >= threshold` (the run's `threshold`); `0` if none
* `flag_rate` – `n_flagged / n_predictions` rounded to 4 decimals, or `0.0` when `n_predictions = 0`
* `avg_score` – average non-NULL score rounded to 4 decimals (`NULL` when there is none)

Sort by `run_id`.

tables.name: ModelRuns
tables.description: One row per trained/deployed model run.

columns.name: threshold
columns.description: Decision threshold: score >= threshold is flagged

tables.name: Predictions
tables.description: Scores produced by a run; at most one per (run, entity).

columns.name: score
columns.description: Model score; NULL if scoring failed

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE ModelRuns (
  run_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  model_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  version    TEXT NOT NULL,
  trained_at TEXT NOT NULL,            -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  threshold  REAL NOT NULL             -- score >= threshold means "flagged"
);
CREATE TABLE Predictions (
  prediction_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id        INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ModelRuns(run_id),
  entity_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  scored_at     TEXT NOT NULL,         -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  score         REAL,                  -- NULL when scoring failed
  UNIQUE (run_id, entity_id)
);
CREATE TABLE GroundTruthLabels (
  entity_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  label      INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (label IN (0,1)),
  labeled_at TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE AlertActions (
  action_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  prediction_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Predictions(prediction_id),
  action        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (action IN ('OPEN','ESCALATED','DISMISSED','CLOSED')),
  actioned_at   TEXT NOT NULL,
  analyst       TEXT NOT NULL
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT r.run_id, r.model_name, r.version, COUNT(p.prediction_id) AS n_predictions, 0 AS n_flagged, 0.0 AS flag_rate, NULL AS avg_score
FROM ModelRuns r
JOIN Predictions p ON p.run_id = r.run_id
GROUP BY r.run_id, r.model_name, r.version;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: run_id, model_name, version, n_predictions, n_flagged, flag_rate, avg_score. One row per run, ordered by run_id.

publicTests.description: Second sample (score equal to threshold counts as flagged)

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT r.run_id, r.model_name, r.version,
       COUNT(p.score) AS n_predictions,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN p.score >= r.threshold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) AS n_flagged,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(p.score) = 0 THEN 0.0
            ELSE ROUND(1.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN p.score >= r.threshold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(p.score), 4) END AS flag_rate,
       ROUND(AVG(p.score), 4) AS avg_score
FROM ModelRuns r
LEFT JOIN Predictions p ON p.run_id = r.run_id
GROUP BY r.run_id, r.model_name, r.version
ORDER BY r.run_id;
solution.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps runs without predictions. COUNT(p.score) ignores NULL scores; the flagged count uses a conditional SUM (COALESCE turns the NULL sum of an empty group into 0). A CASE guards the division. AVG ignores NULLs and returns NULL for an empty group.

rubric.formula: earned = 80 * (sum of weights of passed tests) / (sum of all test weights)
rules: A submission that only compiles/executes without matching expected output earns 0 for that test.
A crash, syntax error or timeout fails only the affected test; remaining tests are still scored.
INNER JOIN drops runs without predictions (LEFT JOIN is required).
COUNT(score) vs COUNT(*) separates NULL scores.
Division-by-zero guard for empty runs.

questions.walkthrough: Run 1 has predictions with scores 0.90, 0.50, 0.20 and one NULL score (ignored) → n_predictions = 3. Its threshold is 0.5, so 0.90 and 0.50 are flagged (a score equal to the threshold counts) → n_flagged = 2, flag_rate = 2/3 = 0.6667, avg_score = 0.5333. Run 4 has no predictions at all but still appears (LEFT JOIN) with 0, 0, 0.0 and a NULL average.
hints: Runs without any predictions must still appear, so which join type do you need from ModelRuns to Predictions?
COUNT(p.score) skips NULL scores, and SUM(CASE WHEN p.score >= r.threshold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts flagged rows.
Guard the division: when COUNT(p.score) = 0 return 0.0. COALESCE turns the NULL sum of an empty group into 0.

questions.title: Alert Rate by Risk Tier
questions.statement:
Using `Transactions`, `AccountProfiles` and `RiskAlerts`, summarise purchases by the account's `risk_tier`.

Consider only transactions with `amount > 0` that belong to an account **having a profile**. A transaction is *flagged* if it has **at least one** row in `RiskAlerts` (any type, resolved or not). Note that a transaction can have several alerts.

Return one row per risk tier that has such transactions:

`risk_tier, txn_count, flagged_count, flag_rate, max_amount`

* `txn_count` – number of distinct qualifying transactions
* `flagged_count` – number of distinct qualifying transactions that are flagged
* `flag_rate` – `flagged_count / txn_count` rounded to 4 decimals
* `max_amount` – largest qualifying amount in the tier

Order tiers `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, `LOW`.

tables.name: Transactions
tables.description: Card/bank transactions; negative amounts are refunds.

tables.name: AccountProfiles
tables.description: At most one profile per account (some accounts have none).

columns.name: avg_monthly_spend
columns.description: Typical monthly spend; NULL if unknown

tables.name: RiskAlerts
tables.description: Zero or more alerts per transaction.

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE Accounts (
  account_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  country       TEXT NOT NULL,
  open_date     TEXT NOT NULL,
  status        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','CLOSED','FROZEN'))
);
CREATE TABLE Transactions (
  txn_id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Accounts(account_id),
  txn_time         TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  amount           REAL NOT NULL,        -- negative = refund
  channel          TEXT NOT NULL,
  merchant_country TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE AccountProfiles (
  account_id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES Accounts(account_id),
  risk_tier          TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (risk_tier IN ('LOW','MEDIUM','HIGH')),
  avg_monthly_spend  REAL,               -- NULL when unknown
  home_country       TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE RiskAlerts (
  alert_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  txn_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Transactions(txn_id),
  alert_type TEXT NOT NULL,
  severity   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (severity IN ('LOW','MEDIUM','HIGH','CRITICAL')),
  created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  resolved   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (resolved IN (0,1))
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT p.risk_tier, COUNT(*) AS txn_count, 0 AS flagged_count, 0.0 AS flag_rate, MAX(t.amount) AS max_amount
FROM Transactions t
JOIN AccountProfiles p ON p.account_id = t.account_id
-- TODO: LEFT JOIN alerts, avoid double counting
GROUP BY p.risk_tier;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: risk_tier, txn_count, flagged_count, flag_rate, max_amount. Order HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW.

hiddenTests.description: Accounts without a profile and transactions without alerts only
Multiple alerts on one transaction must not inflate counts

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT p.risk_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT t.txn_id) AS txn_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.txn_id) AS flagged_count,
       ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.txn_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT t.txn_id), 4) AS flag_rate,
       MAX(t.amount) AS max_amount
FROM Transactions t

questions.title: News Coverage and Market Reaction per Company
questions.statement:
Research wants to see how English-language coverage of each **company** lines up with market activity. Use `NewsArticles`, `SentimentScores`, `Entities` and `MarketEvents`.

For every entity with `entity_type = 'COMPANY'` that has at least one sentiment score on an English article (`language = 'en'`), return:

`entity_name, n_articles, avg_score, confirmed_events`

* `n_articles` – number of sentiment-score rows of that entity on English articles
* `avg_score` – average of those `score` values, rounded to 3 decimals
* `confirmed_events` – the number of **distinct** `MarketEvents` rows of that entity with `event_type = 'PRICE_MOVE'` that happened at or after the publication time of **at least one** of its English articles and no later than 24 hours (inclusive) after that publication time; `0` if none

An event must be counted only once, even if several articles precede it. Sort by `confirmed_events` descending, then `entity_name` ascending.

tables.name: Entities
tables.description: Companies, people and sectors recognised in text.

tables.name: SentimentScores
tables.description: Sentiment of an article towards an entity (one row per article/entity pair).

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE NewsArticles (
  article_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  headline     TEXT NOT NULL,
  source       TEXT NOT NULL,
  published_at TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  language     TEXT NOT NULL           -- ISO code, e.g. 'en'
);
CREATE TABLE Entities (
  entity_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  entity_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  entity_type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (entity_type IN ('COMPANY','PERSON','SECTOR')),
  ticker      TEXT                      -- NULL for non-companies
);
CREATE TABLE SentimentScores (
  article_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES NewsArticles(article_id),
  entity_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Entities(entity_id),
  score      REAL NOT NULL CHECK (score BETWEEN -1 AND 1),
  confidence REAL NOT NULL CHECK (confidence BETWEEN 0 AND 1),
  PRIMARY KEY (article_id, entity_id)
);
CREATE TABLE MarketEvents (
  event_id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  entity_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Entities(entity_id),
  event_time    TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  event_type    TEXT NOT NULL,
  magnitude_pct REAL NOT NULL           -- signed price move in percent
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT e.entity_name, COUNT(*) AS n_articles, 0.0 AS avg_score, 0 AS confirmed_events
FROM Entities e
JOIN SentimentScores s ON s.entity_id = e.entity_id
JOIN NewsArticles a ON a.article_id = s.article_id
-- TODO: English only, companies only; count events with EXISTS (no double counting)
GROUP BY e.entity_name;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: entity_name, n_articles, avg_score, confirmed_events. Ordered by confirmed_events DESC, entity_name ASC.

solution.referenceSolution:
WITH stats AS (
  SELECT s.entity_id, COUNT(*) AS n_articles, ROUND(AVG(s.score), 3) AS avg_score
  FROM SentimentScores s
  JOIN NewsArticles a ON a.article_id = s.article_id
  WHERE a.language = 'en'
  GROUP BY s.entity_id
),
confirmed AS (
  SELECT m.entity_id, COUNT(*) AS confirmed_events
  FROM MarketEvents m
  WHERE m.event_type = 'PRICE_MOVE'
    AND EXISTS (SELECT 1
                FROM SentimentScores s
                JOIN NewsArticles a ON a.article_id = s.article_id
                WHERE s.entity_id = m.entity_id
                  AND a.language = 'en'
                  AND m.event_time >= a.published_at
                  AND m.event_time <= DATETIME(a.published_at, '+1 day'))
  GROUP BY m.entity_id
)
SELECT e.entity_name, st.n_articles, st.avg_score, COALESCE(c.confirmed_events, 0) AS confirmed_events
FROM Entities e
JOIN stats st            ON st.entity_id = e.entity_id
LEFT JOIN confirmed c    ON c.entity_id = e.entity_id
WHERE e.entity_type = 'COMPANY'
ORDER BY confirmed_events DESC, e.entity_name ASC;
solution.explanation: Aggregate sentiment per entity in one CTE and count confirmed events in another so neither join multiplies the other's rows. The EXISTS subquery checks for at least one preceding English article, which guarantees each event is counted once. LEFT JOIN keeps companies with zero confirmed events.

Its PRICE_MOVE events at 2025-03-03 10:00, 2025-03-03 16:00 and 2025-03-06 20:00 each follow an English Acme article within 24 hours → confirmed_events = 3 (the HALT event is not a PRICE_MOVE). import pandas as pd

def clean_ticks(ticks):
    df = ticks.copy()
    df["symbol"] = df["symbol"].str.strip().str.upper()
    df["ts"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ts"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["ts"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["symbol", "ts"], keep="last")
    df = df[df["price"].notna() & (df["price"] > 0) & (df["size"] > 0)]
    df = df.sort_values(["symbol", "ts"], kind="mergesort")
    return df[["symbol", "ts", "price", "size"]].reset_index(drop=True)

questions.title: Daily Monitoring Metrics
questions.statement:
Implement `daily_metrics(preds, threshold)` for a monitoring pipeline.

1. Parse `ts`; drop rows with a missing `score`; define `date` as `ts` normalised to midnight.
2. A row is predicted *positive* when `score >= threshold`. `y_true` is 0/1.
3. For each `date` compute: `n` (rows), `tp`, `fp`, `fn`, `tn` (ints), `precision = tp/(tp+fp)`, `recall = tp/(tp+fn)`, `f1 = 2*tp/(2*tp+fp+fn)` (each `NaN` when its denominator is 0) and `brier` = mean of `(score - y_true)^2`.
4. Return `date, n, tp, fp, fn, tn, precision, recall, f1, brier` sorted by date, default index.

    # TODO

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def daily_metrics(preds, threshold):
    df = preds.copy()
    df["ts"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ts"])
    df = df.dropna(subset=["score"])
    df["date"] = df["ts"].dt.normalize()
    pos = df["score"] >= threshold
    y = df["y_true"] == 1
    df["tp"] = (pos & y).astype("int64")
    df["fp"] = (pos & ~y).astype("int64")
    df["fn"] = (~pos & y).astype("int64")
    df["tn"] = (~pos & ~y).astype("int64")
    df["sq"] = (df["score"] - df["y_true"]) ** 2
    g = df.groupby("date", as_index=False).agg(n=("score", "size"), tp=("tp", "sum"), fp=("fp", "sum"), fn=("fn", "sum"), tn=("tn", "sum"), brier=("sq", "mean"))
    g["precision"] = (g["tp"] / (g["tp"] + g["fp"])).where((g["tp"] + g["fp"]) > 0)
    g["recall"] = (g["tp"] / (g["tp"] + g["fn"])).where((g["tp"] + g["fn"]) > 0)
    den = 2 * g["tp"] + g["fp"] + g["fn"]
    g["f1"] = (2 * g["tp"] / den).where(den > 0)
    return g[["date", "n", "tp", "fp", "fn", "tn", "precision", "recall", "f1", "brier"]].sort_values("date").reset_index(drop=True)

def six_hour_sentiment(scores):

questions.title: IQR Outlier Capping per Symbol
questions.statement:
Implement `clip_outliers(returns)` which caps extreme returns separately for each symbol.

For each `symbol`, with `q1` and `q3` the 25th and 75th percentiles of its non-NaN `ret` (pandas default linear interpolation) and `iqr = q3 - q1`, the fences are `lo = q1 - 1.5*iqr` and `hi = q3 + 1.5*iqr`.

* Symbols with fewer than 4 non-NaN returns are **not** processed: `ret_clipped = ret` and `is_outlier = False`.
* Otherwise `ret_clipped = ret` clipped to `[lo, hi]` and `is_outlier` is `True` exactly when `ret < lo` or `ret > hi`. NaN returns stay NaN with `is_outlier = False`.

Keep the original row order and return `symbol, date, ret, ret_clipped, is_outlier` with default index.

    df = returns.copy()
    # TODO

Constant series: IQR 0 and no outliers

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def clip_outliers(returns):
    df = returns.copy()
    q1 = df.groupby("symbol")["ret"].transform(lambda s: s.quantile(0.25))
    q3 = df.groupby("symbol")["ret"].transform(lambda s: s.quantile(0.75))
    n = df.groupby("symbol")["ret"].transform("count")
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1), q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
    active = n >= 4
    df["ret_clipped"] = df["ret"].where(~active, df["ret"].clip(lower=lo, upper=hi))
    df["is_outlier"] = (active & ((df["ret"] < lo) | (df["ret"] > hi))).astype(bool)
    return df[["symbol", "date", "ret", "ret_clipped", "is_outlier"]].reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: groupby().transform with quantile broadcasts the per-symbol statistics back to the rows, so the original order is kept; Series.clip(lower, upper) takes aligned Series bounds, and boolean masks produce the flag.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def fill_and_returns(prices):
    df = prices.copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    df = df.sort_values(["symbol", "date"], kind="mergesort").reset_index(drop=True)
    df["close"] = df["close"].where(df["close"] > 0)          # non-positive prices are invalid -> missing
    df["close"] = df.groupby("symbol")["close"].ffill()
    prev = df.groupby("symbol")["close"].shift(1)
    df["daily_return"] = df["close"] / prev - 1
    return df[["symbol", "date", "close", "daily_return"]]

questions.title: Balanced Fraud/Normal Windows
questions.statement:
A stream of events is encoded as a string: `'F'` = flagged-fraud event, `'N'` = confirmed-normal event, and any other lowercase letter is an unrelated event. A **window** is a non-empty contiguous substring.

Return the number of windows that contain **exactly as many `'F'` as `'N'` characters** (windows containing neither count, because 0 = 0). Count windows by position: identical substrings at different positions are different windows.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and uppercase 'F' and 'N'

steps: Track balance (+1 for F, −1 for N): prefix balances for 'FNFN' are 0, 1, 0, 1, 0.
Equal balances enclose a balanced window: balance 0 appears 3 times → 3 pairs; balance 1 appears 2 times → 1 pair.
Total = 4 windows: FN, NF, FN, FNFN.

examples.description: 'FFNN' (whole minus x), 'FN' (middle) and 'x' alone are balanced, plus 'FFNNx' itself -> 4 windows
steps: Balance 0 appears 3 times (3 pairs), balance 1 twice (1 pair), balance 2 once (0).
Total = 4: FFNN, FN, x, and FFNNx.

questions.expectedComplexity: O(n) time, O(n) space (prefix balance + hash map)

hiddenTests.description: No F or N at all
All F then all N, n=100000

solution.explanation: Let balance = (#F - #N) over a prefix. A window (i, j] is balanced exactly when prefix balances at i and j are equal. Scan once, keeping a hash map from balance to number of earlier prefixes with that balance; each new prefix adds that many windows.

rubric.formula: earned = 160 * (sum of weights of passed tests) / (sum of all test weights)
rules: A submission that only compiles/executes without matching expected output earns 0 for that test.
A crash, syntax error or timeout fails only the affected test; remaining tests are still scored.
An O(n^2) enumeration passes small tests and fails the n = 100000 tests.
All-neutral strings test that zero-balance windows are counted.
Tests include large inputs: a correct but O(n^2) solution passes the small tests and fails the performance tests (partial credit).

hints: A window is balanced when #F − #N = 0. Track a running balance as you scan.
Two prefixes with the same balance enclose a balanced window.
Keep a dictionary balance → count of earlier prefixes (start with {0: 1}); every new prefix adds that many windows.
